title: X-ray absorption spectroscopic studies of oxygen-deficient double perovskite oxide NdBaCo$_2$O$_{5+δ}$ ($δ\sim 0.65$)
authors: Himanshu Pant, S. Khalid, R. Bindu
abstract: The degree of oxygen vacancy in A-site-doped layered double perovskite oxides can lead to anion vacancy ordering, which subsequently results in distinct superstructures. We have studied oxygen deficient double perovskite oxide, NdBaCo$2$O$_{5+δ}$ ($δ\sim$ 0.65), utilising X-ray absorption near edge structure (XANES) spectroscopy complemented by multiple scattering and first-principles calculations based on density functional theory (DFT+U). The present results establish a direct correlation between oxygen-vacancy distribution, magnetic inhomogeneity, and charge transport in layered cobaltates. Our investigations on the Co K, Ba, and Nd $L_{\mathrm{III}}$ edges suggest that the near-edge spectra, based on the number and shape of the spectral features, indicate the value of $δ$ for the compound under study lies closer to 0.75. The analysis of the Ba $L_{\mathrm{III}}$ edge spectrum confirms the +2 oxidation state for Ba ions. The Co K-edge near-edge spectra suggest the possibility of oxygen vacancies arising at the basal sites in addition to the apical sites. This is counterintuitive to the common understanding that oxygen vacancies usually occur at the apical sites, i.e., in the lanthanide (Nd) layer in these compounds. Such a distribution of oxygen vacancies naturally explains the Griffith phase and the conduction mechanism of variable range hopping observed in the compound. The vacancy distribution, when at the optimum level, can also bring about easier oxygen ion mobility and a more sensitive and faster oxygen sensor. We believe that our results will help in tailoring oxygen-ion mobility and enhancing oxygen-sensing performance.
summary: This work uses X-ray spectroscopy and DFT calculations to probe the electronic structure of oxygen-deficient double perovskites. The key finding is that oxygen vacancies may reside at basal sites, a counterintuitive result that successfully explains the material's variable range hopping conduction and magnetic behavior. This research aids in designing better oxygen sensors and controlling ionic mobility in these complex oxides.
main_problem: The study investigates the relationship between oxygen vacancy distribution, magnetic inhomogeneity, and charge transport in oxygen-deficient double perovskite oxides.
main_result: The XANES analysis suggests oxygen vacancies may occur at basal sites, which explains the observed Griffith phase and variable range hopping conduction mechanism.
method: The research combines X-ray Absorption Near Edge Structure (XANES) spectroscopy with first-principles calculations based on Density Functional Theory (DFT+U) and multiple scattering methods.
model_or_system: The physical system is the oxygen-deficient double perovskite oxide, NdBaCo2O(5+δ), which exhibits complex electronic and magnetic behavior dependent on oxygen stoichiometry.
key_observables: XANES spectral features (Co K, Ba LIII, Nd LIII edges), oxidation states, oxygen vacancy distribution (apical vs. basal sites), and magnetic transition temperatures.
important_parameters: Oxygen stoichiometry (δ), temperature (T), and the local coordination environment of the Co ions.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes that the local structure, probed by XANES, can reveal the true vacancy distribution, even when conflicting with common understanding.
figures_summary: Figures likely show calculated and measured XANES spectra across different edges, PDOS plots detailing Co 3d/4p hybridization, and structural models illustrating vacancy ordering.
paper_structure: The paper follows a structure of characterizing the material via synthesis and bulk measurements (XRD, Magnetometry), followed by detailed local electronic structure analysis using XANES and DFT+U calculations to pinpoint the role of oxygen vacancies.
why_interesting: The strong correlation between structural defects (vacancies) and emergent electronic/magnetic properties is a hallmark of strongly correlated electron systems, making it relevant for understanding charge transport in complex oxides.
